[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: 'length' is something you ask for, like s.length() for a String, and in everyday counting 'length 10' suggests the last item is number 10. Java rule: a.length is a final field written without parentheses, equal to the number of elements, so the last index is a.length-1.
[1] misconception (M) -> ArrayHasLengthMethod: wrong rule: You call length() instead of using the length field. Right rule: An array's size is the field a.length, written without parentheses; length() is a String method.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ArrayHasLengthMethod: Points to LT: a.length is read every time the loop test i < a.length runs. Inconsistent application: the trace uses a.length as the last valid index on some passes (as if the test were <=). (here mixing in: "you call length() instead of using the length field")
[3] misconception (M) -> ArrayLengthCannotBeZero: wrong rule: An array cannot have length 0. Right rule: new int[0] is a legal array with length 0; args is such an array when no arguments are typed.

[0] names_the_element (N): Identity: a.length is the public final instance field that every array has, holding its number of elements.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Declarative: the length of array a is written a.length (no parentheses); it equals the size given at creation, may be zero, cannot be assigned, and the last element is a[a.length-1].

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Sequencing: a is evaluated first (a null a throws NullPointerException), then the length field of the array a refers to now is read. In 'for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++)' it is re-read at each test.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Result: an int >= 0 equal to the number of elements: new double[8].length is 8, {1, 2, 3}.length is 3, and the last element is a[a.length-1].
[2] one_step_execution (OS): State transition: reading a.length changes nothing. Assigning 'a.length = 5' is impossible (a final field), so only making a refer to a different array changes the value later read as a.length.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): The n given to new becomes a.length and stays fixed for that array object.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): args is an ordinary String[], so args.length is its length field and counts the command-line arguments (0 when none are typed).
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan/role: a fixed value (Sajaniemi) that lets code adapt to any array size instead of a hard-coded magic number, e.g. loop bounds and the last element.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ArrayHasLengthMethod: Conservation: for a given array object a.length never changes, so loops bounded by a.length stay correct when the array is created with a different size. Reassigning a to another array changes a.length.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Applicability: use a.length wherever code must follow the array's real size (loop bounds, last element, copying); use a[i].length for each row of a possibly ragged 2-D array; use s.length() for Strings.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: length is a field, not a method. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: a.length() is written for an array (cannot find symbol: method length())
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: length is final and cannot be assigned. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: 'a.length = n;' (cannot assign a value to final variable length)
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The last valid index is a.length-1. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: a[a.length] or a loop with i <= a.length (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)

A traversal loop runs its index from 0 while it is below a.length, so it visits every element once.
